Stated Claim / Post Context:
Trump lashes out against 'incompetent' Gavin Newsom for commuting death sentences of 548 inmates in California: 'disaster for justice in America'

In one of his final acts as outgoing governor, the Democrat announced on November 5 that he is sparing every murder on death row in the Golden State.

Actual Article Body:
By VICTOR HELLER, US REPORTER

Published:  08:20 AEDT, 15 November 2026   |  Updated:  08:21 AEDT, 15 November 2026

Donald Trump has launched a fresh attack against his arch-enemy Gavin Newsom, whose decision to commute the death sentences of 548 inmates the president labeled a 'disaster for justice in America.'

In one of his final acts as outgoing governor, the Democrat announced on November 5 that he is sparing every murderer on death row in California.

The move sparked massive backlash, especially from conservatives like president Trump, who condemned Newsom for halting the death penalty for 'some of the worst cold blooded murderers to have ever lived.'

He further dubbed the decision a 'disaster for justice in America' as 'the family members of those who were so viciously killed are, rightfully, devastated.'

Newsom himself acknowledged that the prisoners he decided to give a second chance at life caused 'indescribable suffering' but also argued 'the state cannot morally kill them.'

'State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us,' he wrote in a letter to California residents.

'I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.'

As the decision engulfed Newsom in controversy, he unveiled that it was the murder case of a 12-year-old girl that convinced him of granting clemency to every death row inmate.

Donald Trump lashed out against California governor Gavin Newsom for his decision to commute every convicted killer's death sentence

The president took his fury to social media and described Newsom's move as a 'disaster for justice in America'

Newsom announced his decision in a letter to California residents earlier this month and continues to deal with strong backlash for the move

Polly Klaas, a school girl from Petaluma, was kidnapped in the city north of San Francisco and murdered in 1993.

Her killer, Richard Allen Davis, was caught and sentenced to death.

But when Newsom met with Klaas's two sisters in October, they convinced him that execution is not the right path as it does not bring victims back, heal grieving families or restore a sense of justice, he said.

Instead, their words moved the politician so much that he later described the encounter as one of the most profound meetings of his life and crucial to his recent ruling.
